title: Tenant sidecar enforcement for per-tenant throughput contracts and noisy-neighbor mitigation
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Goal: Implement a lightweight per-tenant sidecar enforcement layer that sits adjacent to tenant GPU slots and enforces agreed throughput contracts, mitigates noisy neighbors, and provides a clean backpressure signal to autoscaling and API routing. This ticket covers design + PoC + integration with autoscaler and telemetry.

Background: Existing fleet-level throttle and lane-slicing mechanisms provide good macro-level guarantees but leave blind spots during transient bursts and mixed workloads (memory-bound vs compute-bound). Several incidents showed tail latency spikes when a co-located tenant performs heavy KV-cache invalidations or large-batch requests. We need a tenant-local enforcement primitive that: 1) enforces per-tenant sustained throughput and burst budgets, 2) surfaces precise backpressure to the request ingress, and 3) cooperates with cluster autoscale and eviction playbooks.

Proposed approach:
- Sidecar responsibilities: per-tenant token-bucket rate limiter (requests/sec + tokens-per-tokenized-token), short-term burst reservoir, realtime telemetry export (per-request latency histogram, GPU memory pressure, kernel busy fraction).
- Enforcement mechanisms: soft-limits implemented in-process for fast rejection + backpressure; hard-limits enforced via cgroup v2 for CPU/vGPU or via NVIDIA MIG caps where available. Eviction escalation path: soft-reject -> degrade to smaller model variant (routing fallback) -> mark for preemptive eviction if sustained over threshold.
- Autoscale integration: sidecar emits a compact health/event stream to the dedicated autoscaler: (consumption_rate, burst_remaining, memory_pressure, tail_95_latency). Autoscaler uses a predictive 30s window to request scale-up (warm new slot) when predicted capacity < configured SLO headroom. Maintain a minimal "burst credit" ledger per tenant to allow short bursts without immediate scale-up.
- Noisy neighbor detection: correlate sudden increases in kernel busy fraction + host-level GPU SM utilization with tenant's own request patterns. If heavy resource use is observed without corresponding token consumption (e.g., large background salvages, maintenance jobs), classify as noisy neighbor behavior and throttle at the sidecar while tagging owner for investigation.
- Observability + runbooks: expose tenant QoS dashboard (per-tenant burst ledger, recent soft/hard rejects, autoscale decisions). Add runbook: steps to verify sidecar logs, reproduce with synthetic load, and safe-playbook to migrate tenant to dedicated hard-sliced pool.
- Rollout plan: PoC on dev cluster (one host with two tenants), then graduated canary on dedicated fleet (5% of production tenants), then 25% with A/B on slow-path fallback. Metrics to validate: successful QoS adherence (99.9% of requests within contracted throughput), reduction in cross-tenant tail latency events by 70%, false-positive throttles < 1%.

Tradeoffs & open questions:
- Latency vs enforcement granularity: per-request checks in sidecar add ~0.2-0.8ms; acceptable for most workloads but may impact extremely latency-sensitive flows. Consider sampling or fast-path bypass for pinned SLO tenants.
- Complexity of cgroup + MIG integration across clouds: MIG availability varies by GPU type and cloud. Start with cgroup v2 CPU/GPU-throttling where supported; provide software-only fallback enforced in sidecar for others.
- Billing semantics for burst credits: need product/finance alignment on whether short bursts beyond committed throughput are billed at overage rates or consumed from reserved burst credits.

Acceptance criteria:
- Sidecar binary + container image built and deployed in dev cluster, with end-to-end tests for soft/hard reject paths.
- Autoscaler consumes sidecar events and triggers warm-up requests in PoC.
- Dashboards showing per-tenant ledger and recent enforcement events.
- Performance tests proving <1% additional p95 latency for standard generation workloads under typical token sizes.

Next steps: finalize sidecar API (token semantics + health stream), implement PoC enforcement loop, instrument avail flags to autoscaler team, and prepare PRD for finance billing treatment.
comments: 2025-02-11 Aisha Patel: Scoping doc uploaded to Confluence. Key decision: use token-bucket measured in normalized model tokens (tokenized tokens) rather than bytes so that billing and SLO align with API metrics.
2025-02-12 Miguel Ortega: Drafted PoC plan. Starting with an in-process rate limiter plus a cgroup v2 hard cap toggle. Will prototype in runtime sandbox. Assigned to ENG-31209 for scheduler hooks.
2025-02-13 Priya Nair (PM): Please ensure autoscaler integration has a clear safety window to avoid oscillation. Suggest adding a 15s cool-down and minimum warmup capacity of 1 slot per tenant.
2025-02-14 Design Review (Liam Chen): UX note: dashboards need a clear signal for 'burst-credit remaining' and a timeline view of enforcement. We'll add mockups to the Confluence page.

2025-02-15 Engineering sync: Decided to implement two enforcement tiers (fast-path soft in sidecar, slow-path hard via cgroup/MIG). Miguel to open runtime PR for health stream formatting. Reference PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1247

2025-02-17 Miguel Ortega: PoC container image built. Metrics export uses protobuf over unix socket to minimize overhead. Observed ~0.4ms median extra latency on small-gen tests. Starting canary rollout plan documentation.
2025-02-18 SRE (Elena Popov): Add a safety toggle that allows control plane to opt tenants out of sidecar enforcement during incident DB migrations. SRE will own runbook updates.
